ranking.rationale: Age is a strong, semantically stable predictor for lead burden and related exposure patterns, and is less likely than year or demographic identifiers to encode domain-specific shortcuts or leakage.
Gender is a broadly stable demographic predictor that can add signal beyond age without directly encoding survey year or likely domain-specific artifacts.

Education is a strong, semantically stable predictor of lead exposure risk and related health behaviors, adding information beyond age and sex without directly encoding the domain split or obvious leakage.

Marital status is a relatively stable socioeconomic/life-course signal that can add predictive value beyond age, sex, and education without directly encoding survey year or obvious domain-specific artifacts.

Race/ethnicity is a strong, semantically meaningful predictor of lead exposure risk and related health disparities that can remain informative across domains, whereas year and birthplace are more likely to act as domain or cohort proxies.

Country of birth can capture persistent exposure and socioeconomic differences relevant to lead burden, while being less directly tied to the split mechanism than year; it should add stable predictive signal beyond age, sex, education, marital status, and race/ethnicity.
The year can capture broad secular trends in lead exposure and survey-era shifts that may remain predictive across splits, though it is also somewhat domain-specific.
